overview: Dominica’s history includes Indigenous pottery, plantation slavery, resistance and an independent republic established in 1978. Its earlier archaeological sites and continuing craft traditions reveal more than changes of government. Creole music, dance and language research show communities making and teaching knowledge across generations.

periods.title: Contested colonial rule and slavery
periods.summary: Britain captured Dominica in 1761 and received it by treaty in 1763. French administration returned from 1778 to 1784. Sugar and coffee production depended on enslaved labour under colonial rule.

periods.title: Abolition and compulsory apprenticeship
periods.summary: Abolition in 1834 was followed by apprenticeship, which continued to compel labour. Its termination in 1838 was a separate step toward freedom.

periods.title: Freedom within a colonial society
periods.summary: Apprenticeship ended in 1838. Emancipation did not make Dominica an independent country.

periods.title: Communal territory under colonial rule
periods.summary: The Kalinago Territory received official recognition in 1903. British recognition of the chief’s office was interrupted from 1930 to 1953, while community leadership continued.

periods.title: Associated statehood
periods.summary: Dominica became an associated state in March 1967. This constitutional stage preceded full political independence.

periods.title: The independent republic
periods.summary: On 3 November 1978, association with Britain ended and the Commonwealth of Dominica became a sovereign republic.

sections.title: Discoveries and the limits of the evidence

items.text: At Woodford Hill, Andre Samuel found two nearly complete Cayo pottery jars in an eroding headland in 2004. A later survey recovered pottery, stone flakes, charcoal, fish bones and shells behind an old warehouse. These finds illuminate manufacture and food use, but older material was mixed with modern glass, metal and ceramics.

At the Eden River mouth, pottery includes incised and modelled decoration, possible griddle fragments and pieces assigned to different ceramic traditions. The mixed deposit records repeated use of the locality. It cannot be treated as one household assemblage or used to prove that a change in pottery meant one people replaced another.

Jacko escaped from enslavement at Castle Comfort Estate and established a refuge in the mountainous interior near Belles, at the place now called Jacko Flats. His community sheltered people escaping coastal plantations. He was killed by colonial Rangers in July 1814 during the suppression of Maroon resistance.

Dominica’s emancipation observances remember both legal abolition in 1834 and the end of apprenticeship in 1838. Lectures, exhibitions, drumming and bèlè performances connect public history with artistic practice. Remembering the two dates separately helps explain why the first legal change did not immediately end coerced work.

Sandra Thomas made a wicker-plaited larouma-fibre basket in Dominica in 2002. The Smithsonian records both the artist and the material; its staff member Susan Secakuku bought the basket directly from Thomas the following year. This is documented contemporary craft, with an identified maker, rather than an anonymous archaeological object.

Kalinago Barana Aute presents craft, cassava-bread making and canoe-building demonstrations led by community practitioners. Its model cultural village includes a covered communal meeting place. These activities make skills available for teaching and paid cultural work; the buildings are a modern interpretation of heritage, not surviving ancient houses.

The Kalinago account of their territory describes colonial land sales and dispossession, followed by retreat toward the east coast. Recognition of communal land in 1903 did not begin their history. Even when colonial authorities suspended the chief’s office, community members continued to recognize elders as leaders.

Pearle Christian’s description of traditional instruments explains how a tambou bèlè uses rope and pegs to tension its skin: greater tension raises the pitch. Drum bodies can be made from kegs, metal cans or hollowed trunks. The instrument joins practical knowledge of materials with the demands of dance and collective performance.

The bamboo flute has a blowing hole and six finger holes, allowing the player to change pitch. In jing ping music, the accordion supplies a reed-driven melody. These instruments show different routes to a local sound: shaping plant material into an instrument and adapting an imported instrument to Dominican performance.

Daryl Phillip’s 1994 account describes quadrilles as coordinated sequences for four couples. Musicians must understand the steps and change rhythm to suit them. Sequence names vary with place and language: Woodford Hill uses Kokoy terms alongside the Creole names found elsewhere. The dances preserve local differences within a shared form.

Mabel Cissie Caudeiron composed Creole songs, founded the Kairi Artistic Troupe and researched music, dress and dance. She also helped organize the 1965 National Day celebrations. Her work brought practices associated with ordinary Dominican life onto public stages and into written accounts, years before political independence.

Established in 1981, Kommité pou Etid Kwéyòl organized literacy classes and the first Jounen Kwéyòl celebration that October. Its publications include proverbs, riddles called timtim, and a Kwéyòl-English dictionary. This work treats a spoken community language as a medium for reading, teaching and research.

ending.text: Colonial association with Britain ended in 1978, when Dominica became an independent republic. Kalinago community life and Creole cultural institutions continue. The end of a map interval is not the end of these communities or of the country.
